entry.title: Xi-Trump summit signals a shifting order India must learn to navigate
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Xi-Trump summit signals a shifting order India must learn to navigateXi-Trump summit signals a shifting order India must learn to navigate

The trilateral summit raises the prospect of a bipolar US-China condominium, with Russia not quite in the same league and India facing a more challenging geopolitical landscape

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Shyam Saran6 min read Last Updated : Nov 27 2026 | 11:12 PM ISTChinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and United States President Donald Trump held an unprecedented trilateral summit on November 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. The summit released a Trilateral Peace Declaration with four points of agreement whose implications are serious and should invite greater attention.  That a summit among the three leaders took place at all was remarkable, and to treat it as a mere photo-op misses its significance. Its outcome should be assessed together with the outcomes of the earlier bilateral meeting between Xi Jinping and Mr Trump and between Mr Putin and Mr Trump in advance of their trilateral summit. The more important bilateral meeting was undoubtedly between Mr Xi and Mr Trump, the readout of which has some important elements:  One, there is a reiteration of “constructive strategic stability” as a shared objective, but now there is a reference to the two sides formulating a “constructive strategic stability action plan”. This goes beyond mere rhetoric. How such an action plan will be negotiated and what its content would be remain to be seen but should be watched closely.  Two, the language on Taiwan suggests that China believes that US policy is moving in the right direction.  “On the Taiwan issue, the US must keep doing the right thing to avoid the emergence of great turbulence in the China-US relationship.”  This implies that China is encouraged by the trend in US approach to Taiwan and is now more confident of achieving the goal of reunification. By the same token, this is bad news for the East and Southeast Asian partners of the US because a Taiwan unified with China will change the geopolitical landscape of the Indo-Pacific region. Japan and South Korea will be the most affected. The voices pressing for going nuclear are rising in both countries in response.  China is comfortable with Mr  Trump and sees opportunities to advance its influence and role particularly in Asia, while the latter is still President. The Chinese readout says that Xi Jinping considers that “the guiding role of the diplomacy between the US and Chinese heads of state is irreplaceable.”  Xi Jinping is reported to have said that “the US is very powerful; China is also very powerful” and that the two countries should “jointly lead and promote world peace and stability.”   It is the US-China bilateral that set the stage for the trilateral, but Russia is not regarded by either as being in the same league. The feared condominium, if it emerges, will be bipolar, not tripolar. The photo-op was important for Russia, to be seen as a great power, though it is not.  Let us analyse the Trilateral Peace Declaration whose four points were:  One, reform of the United Nations, although it was not clear what they intended in this respect. The three signatories are referred to as “permanent members” of the Security Council, but they completely ignore the two other permanent members — France and the United Kingdom. The US allies no longer count.  Two, the three countries plan to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. This means the end of energy sanctions against Russia. India will breathe a sigh of relief and will continue purchasing Russian oil.  Three, the International Criminal Court (ICC) is condemned for overstepping its jurisdiction and violating “the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials”. This was an easy point of agreement as none of the three countries is a member of the ICC. Mr Putin smiled broadly when this was mentioned by Mr Trump. He has been indicted by the ICC for criminal behaviour in the assault against Ukraine.  Four, reaffirmation of an earlier declaration of the five permanent members, all nuclear weapon states, that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”. This is reassuring specially in the wake of Russia threatening the use of nuclear weapons in the Ukraine War. There is also a commitment that the three countries would “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons”.  This falls short of the US proposal for nuclear arms control talks among the three nuclear weapon states with the largest arsenals, which China has so far refused to join. But talks on nuclear risk reduction could be a useful starting point. The reference to cooperation on non-proliferation is interesting. This could be a veiled reference to the Iran nuclear issue as well as the North Korea nuclear issue. For China, it could well be alluding to the threat of Japan and South Korea going nuclear, which would pose a greater challenge to China but may not be welcome to the US either.   We should remember that even during the height of the Cold War, both the US and the then Soviet Union found common cause in preventing other countries from developing nuclear weapons. The discriminatory Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) was the result. As a nuclear weapon state that has rejected the NPT, India should watch how this element of cooperation develops among the three countries and whether there may be constraints put on countries like India.   Could there be revival of calls for the universalisation of the NPT? China has opposed India’s membership of the Nuclear Suppliers’ Group and was virtually the last country to join the consensus in the NSG on the waiver provided to India in 2008 from the norms of the group prohibiting nuclear cooperation with countries non-signatories to the NPT. Could China try to reverse the waiver or seek it for Pakistan? How would the US react in the changed geopolitical circumstances? Could Mr Trump oblige his favourite field marshal from Pakistan?  A great deal can happen in the two years left of Mr Trump’s tenure, and the Chinese and the Russians are determined to make the most of the opportunities this offers to them. When facts on the ground change, it is difficult to reverse course even if a new political dispensation takes charge in Washington in 2029.  The next Xi-Trump summit is slated for mid-December this year when the G-20 summit is hosted by the US in Miami. There could even be another trilateral summit. China is gaining in influence, Russia is masking its decline, and the US is ceding space that would be difficult to retrieve. This is the challenging terrain that India must learn to navigate as we head into the new year. 
The writer is a former foreign secretary   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Donald Trump Vladimir Putin Xi Jinping US China BS Opinion

entry.title: Tata Sons should choose its future rather than face a forced listing
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tata Sons should choose its future rather than face a forced listingTata Sons should choose its future rather than face a forced listing

Tata Sons should not be compelled to list, as an IPO could affect the group's corporate soul, culture and values

premium

R Gopalakrishnan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 27 2026 | 11:52 PM ISTThe Tata group has a reorganisation idea to meet statutory norms for listing through an initial public offering (IPO). Is it not sensible to let the group adapt if it does not wish to list — that too, under duress of regulation? Don’t compel Tata Sons to list. Let the people there decide voluntarily. The group is a national jewel and should be allowed to continue to play its role in India’s aspirations.  This article is replete with global business examples, reflecting that concerns are real, and not retired directors’ emotions.  Tata Trusts and Tata Sons must converge regarding an IPO. Harmony does not require sameness and can be achieved even without complete convergence.  The idea that a company possesses a soul (spirit/culture) is quite Indian, distinct from a transactional perspective. A corporate soul is mauled by a traumatic shock.  Whether Tata Sons should do an IPO is of supreme concern to retired and senior Tata employees. The organisation should do an internal survey to assess opinion on whether an IPO could diminish “Tataness”, especially under compulsion.  My enquiry among retirees and senior Tata employees suggests deep concern about mandatory listing. They have fears that their “spiritual holding company” will be hurt. They have observed the behaviour and values of leaders when the firm had acted well beyond what the law required. The firm’s responses had emanated from its soul rather than the laws. These senior employees now find the idea of an IPO as unacceptable — quite a red flag, not to be ignored!  Soul, spirit, and culture are nurtured by leaders’ behaviour when confronted with a dharma sankat (dilemma). For example, in 1922, when Dorabji Tata raised money, placing his wife’s Jubilee Diamond as collateral to pay  Tisco (now Tata Steel) workers; in the 1940s, when J R D Tata would not close down a loss-making Mithapur factory of Tata Chemicals because “where Tata goes, it raises the hopes of people in the community”; in 2001, when Ratan Tata assured repayment to every Tata Finance investor after an unfortunate fraud. All these examples cost Tata Sons some reputation and lots of money. It is worth reflecting whether Tata Sons could act consistently in the same way if it is a listed company in the future. The requirements of its other shareholders would influence the decision.  The soul also manifests in non-financial ways — humane ways when unforeseen calamities hit a Tata company: How JRD visited every affected family in the unfortunate fire in Jamshedpur in 1989; how Ratan Tata visited every injured person at hospital after the 2008 terror attack; how N Chandrasekaran and Noel Tata visited the accident site after the Air India crash at Ahmedabad last year.  Modern techniques of risk analyses do not evaluate the effect of frayed employee feelings. Companies are “live” entities. Reactions to a collective slight can create uncontrollable waves of turmoil and uncertainty. Remember the merger of Jet Airways and Sahara? Remember the Essar group’s failed takeover of Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank, creating enormous angst among the Nadar community? You want more evidence that the corporate soul can be damaged in the eyes of the employees?  Here goes, not surprisingly most of them from the Anglo-American world.  Messing with the soul: When a mission-driven SAIC (Science Applications International Corporation), deeply committed to employee ownership, did an IPO in 2013, Robert Beyster, the founder, lost his mission. When mission-driven Ventura was taken over in 2021 by PMI (Phillip Morris International), a lung-health company quite ridiculously got absorbed into a cigarette company.    Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) was founded in 1926. It believed it was a national institution and behaved as such. For all those years, ICI flourished. Sixty years later, with Anglo-American ideas on the primacy of shareholder capitalism, management came under pressure to improve quarterly performance and increase margins and cash generation.  ICI gradually moved from “what technologies should we invent for the future” to “which businesses generate the highest returns today?” Its soul was damaged. ICI does not exist any longer.  “How Johnson & Johnson (J&J) nearly lost its soul” is a story associated with the legendary chief executive officer James Burke. By 1980, Burke believed that J&J was fast becoming a financially driven firm. He deeply desired the firm to course-correct to Robert Wood’s “Our Credo”, crafted in 1943. In 1982, when the Tylenol crisis gripped J&J, Burke acted in accordance with “Our Credo” of 1943: Recall all the 31 million bottles of stock and incur massive losses. The crisis demonstrated how character survived in J&J.  Daimler-Benz merged with Chrysler in 1998. Officially described as a “merger of equals”, many Chrysler employees soon realised that Daimler was running the combined company. Differences in German and American management styles created friction.  Over a few years, senior Chrysler leaders left, particularly as the expected synergies failed to materialise. Daimler eventually sold Chrysler in 2007 in desperation. It was tumultuous for employees and shareholders while the merchant bankers counted their spoils.  AOL merged with Time Warner in 2001. Time Warner managers resented being controlled by AOL, whose valuation in their opinion was inflated. The cultures clashed. AOL was fast-moving and aggressive while Time Warner was a traditional media company. Internal conflicts increased and the synergies never emerged. The merger became one of the most famous failures in corporate history. Resentment grew when the acquired side believed that the acquirer lacked the substance to justify control. HP merged with Compaq in 2002. This merger was Carly Fiorina’s last corporate hurrah. The merger was a subject of my book Crash, 2018. Many HP traditionalists and founding-family members opposed the merger. Compaq employees often felt their identity was being absorbed by HP. Years of integration challenges and cultural clashes continued, resulting in high turnover and prolonged internal debate. The cultural resentment lasted for years.  India should not import “germs” from the Anglo-American bloodstream, especially when the Tata group itself is willing to adapt by returning loans and reorganise in line with policy.  
The writer is a business commentator and has written 21 books on human behaviour and enterprise leadership. entry.title: AI-assisted piracy puts Grand Theft Auto's business model to test
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AI-assisted piracy puts Grand Theft Auto's business model to testAI-assisted piracy puts Grand Theft Auto's business model to test

Over 512 million units of the core games have been sold, and there are countless spin-offs too

premium

Every iteration of the GTA series has been cutting-edge, leveraging the best technologies of the day

Devangshu Datta4 min read Last Updated : Nov 27 2026 | 11:39 PM ISTEver since the first release in 1997, Grand Theft Auto (GTA) has been among the most popular videogames. GTA players wander around fictional landscapes, stealing cars, shooting people, and generally committing mayhem. GTA is a prime example of the products that make gaming by far the most valuable segment of the entertainment industry.  It is estimated that global gaming (inclusive of hardware, live stream revenues, and advertising) will generate $560 billion in revenues in 2026. Just games (excluding hardware, streaming and ads) will generate $215 billion. For context, the global movie industry will earn a piddling $126 billion this year.     A large chunk of the world’s 3.7 billion gamers play GTA. Over 512 million units of the core games have been sold, and there are countless spin-offs too. The GTA series has always been admired for its state-of-the-art quality. Every iteration of the GTA series has been cutting-edge, leveraging the best technologies of the day. Digital historians can map the evolution of the digital industry simply by the way GTA went from being 2D (two-dimensional) to 3D to HD (high-definition).  It has been claimed (with more than a grain of truth) that GTA is the United Kingdom’s most successful export of the 21st century. It was developed by Scottish gamers at Rockstar North, originally an Edinburgh company, which is now the subsidiary of United States’ Rockstar Games. It has also always been controversial due to its violent, amoral storylines.  Players role-play as criminals, rising through the ranks of organised crime “mobs”, with many missions and side stories. Apart from the violence and amorality, GTA has also been criticised for the demeaning ways it depicts many (not all) women characters. The game features sex-workers, “gangsters’ molls”, and realistically depicted strip clubs. The timelines range from historic, from the 1920s onwards, to fictional near-future settings.  The locations are fictional in terms of names (Liberty City, San Fiero, Los Santos). But GTA is mostly set in US cities like New York, New Jersey, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Las Vegas, and Miami. London and Scottish locales also appear. The cities are rendered in granular detail using GPS, and 3D maps of real places. Scientists have taken GTA locales, and run simulations of flooding to see how they are affected by weather. The renders are that good (and scientists are that nerdy).     The sixth iteration of GTA — GTA6 — released on November 19, and it has immediately led to accusations of theft and piracy. This, too, is a paradigm driven by cutting-edge technology. Rockstar has always made its money with a business model involving what many gamers consider sharp practice. First, they release a version for consoles. Then, several months later, they release a version for the personal computer (PC). Gamers who need their GTA fix end up buying it twice, or even thrice. GTA6 was released on November 19 for the Xbox Series X|S and Playstation5 (PS5/Pro) platforms, with prices ranging from €60-90 equivalent. Less than a week later, there are excellent versions available for the PC. And, these are free.  Rockstar didn’t release them. Gamers and vibe coders using artificial intelligence (AI) pulled GTA6 from Xbox consoles and managed to get it to run on Windows PCs. A hacker group called Cyberleek had hacked into Rockstar, and leaked a large portion of the code for the Xbox version of the game. Xbox is a Microsoft product and runs on Windows. Gamers and vibe coders recompiled to make it run natively on high-end Windows PCs.  Here’s a technical point. A console game (or any native android app for that matter) can always be run on a desktop PC by using an emulator. Emulation makes the desktop’s hardware behave like the console’s hardware (or a mobile). But it radically slows the PC down, which is a dealbreaker for a game like GTA. Instead, if the code is taken apart and recompiled, the computer needn’t throttle itself. Recompilation is essentially what the company would do to create a PC-native version. It used to take expertise, intimate coding knowledge and many man-hours.  Vibe coders can now use AI to do this. There’s no official estimate of how many tokens were expended on which AI to do this recompilation. But the unofficial builds work smoothly and it’s been less than a week. Of course, there’s a high risk that these PC versions are also seeded with malware. And, of course, this is illegal. But surely you didn’t expect gamers who spend their days pretending to be mobsters to be restrained by moral considerations?

entry.title: The boy who died in Harry Potter gets a licence to survive (and kill)
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The boy who died in Harry Potter gets a licence to survive (and kill)The boy who died in Harry Potter gets a licence to survive (and kill)

Now, he faces an even greater challenge: That of being James Bond. It certainly marks a new chapter of a long-standing cultural institution

premium

Robert Pattinson

Atanu Biswas5 min read Last Updated : Nov 27 2026 | 10:48 PM IST“Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.” With this message on social media, the British Royal Family has welcomed actor Robert Pattinson after he was announced as the next James Bond. In reality, however, Pattinson has been welcomed into the domain of immortality through the character of an iconic spy.  Pattinson has a strange on-screen relationship with death. As a wizard, he died young. In his first big-screen appearance in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, the young actor had played an ideal Hogwarts student. However, Cedric died by the Killing Curse cast by Peter Pettigrew — or Wormtail — based on Lord Voldemort’s orders. His death was indeed an introduction to a harsh, unforgiving reality in the magical world of Harry Potter.  Then came Twilight, the 2008 American romantic fantasy film directed by Catherine Hardwicke. Within a few years of Cedric’s death, Pattinson played Edward Cullen — a young, handsome, wealthy vampire. Well, all vampires are immortal. Thus, as Edward Cullen in Twilight, Pattinson conquered death and possessed eternal youth. The audience was captivated by a combination of teenage romance, jealousy, attraction, and supernatural elements. And, not to forget that, despite being a vampire, Edward could easily be an ideal lover!  Subsequently, in his acting career, Pattinson must have wanted to come out of that image. He chose to portray unsettling, complex, and, at times, almost unrecognisable characters. In Josh and Benny Safdie’s Good Time (2017), Pattinson was a small-time criminal, and in Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse (2019), he played a troubled nineteenth-century lighthouse keeper stranded at a remote New England outpost.  Then, earlier this year, in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, Pattinson played Antinous, the main antagonist and arrogant ringleader of Queen Penelope’s suitors. Here he again faces death. In Homer’s epic, Antinous is the first suitor to be killed by an arrow to the throat, but Matt Damon, Nolan’s Odysseus, saves him for last.  Meanwhile, in Matt Reeves’ 2022 movie, The Batman, Bruce Wayne was not a superhuman. Pattinson portrayed Bruce Wayne as a broken “weirdo”. He was haunted by the memory of his parents’ killing in his childhood. His battle against criminals was like an unfinished attempt to heal that wound deep inside. Bruce Wayne had wealth, he relied on technology and training, and he possessed a profound sense of melancholy. In fact, Pattinson himself spoke out about the “overwhelming sadness” of The Batman.  Now, he faces an even greater challenge: That of being James Bond. It certainly marks a new chapter of a long-standing cultural institution. Born from the novels of Ian Fleming, James Bond first appeared on screen in 1962’s Dr. No. “Bond. James Bond” in Sean Connery’s voice has since become the signature catchphrase of the fictional MI6 agent 007 and also an iconic fixture of popular culture. Subsequently, five more actors, namely George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig, have brought their own chemistry and interpretation to the character. Each of these actors maintained the character’s foundational and distinguishable traits. But, in the process, they also left the distinct imprint of their own era.  The main attraction of Bond, certainly, is not just in espionage but in the dream of an extraordinary, impossible lifestyle. Sometimes he travels in an Aston Martin, sometimes in a submarine. His tuxedo remains virtually pristine even amidst explosions, the ice in his martini glass never melts, and the Bond girls keep us amazed. And his dangerous villains invariably pause to deliver quite long speeches before attempting to kill him; Bond’s survival depends much on the verbosity of his villains, too, along with his own skills!  Some believe that Connery is the definitive Bond. For some, it’s Moore. In fact, Sean Connery’s Bond had a dangerous, masculine charm, while Roger Moore brought a sense of humour and a lighter touch. Timothy Dalton, however, portrayed a sterner, tougher Bond, and Pierce Brosnan brought back a sense of glamour. The new generation thinks that Daniel Craig is the real Bond. Craig’s Bond, of course, is far more human.  Pattinson would be playing the role of the iconic spy when the very definition of a male cinematic hero has been undergoing a change. Today’s hero may not be a confident, formidable, and emotionless man as earlier. Rather, today’s audience might prefer vulnerabilities in a hero. Thus, as Pattinson intends to play Bond in a renewed worldview, he has quite a complex and formidable task ahead. He has already played diverse characters in his acting career. Now, will he be able to become both resolutely firm, loyal, and unwavering in purpose and simultaneously fragile as James Bond?  Cedric has died, Edward can’t die, Antinous faces a miserable death, and Batman lives with the memory of death. But Pattinson now holds a “license to kill” (and thrill!). And a “license to survive,” too!

entry.title: FPI buying lifts markets, but India's external outlook remains uncertain
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / FPI buying lifts markets, but India's external outlook remains uncertainFPI buying lifts markets, but India's external outlook remains uncertain

FPI buying offers relief, but India must strengthen its external position amid global uncertainties and volatile capital flows

premium

Representative image for Foreign portfolio investors

Rajesh Kumar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 9:55 PM ISTForeign portfolio investors (FPIs) have made a strong comeback in Indian stock markets, buying stocks worth over $15 billion on a net basis so far in November. This has changed sentiment not only in the stock market, but also in the currency market.  In the stock market, the benchmark Nifty 50 has gained about 12 per cent in November, while the rupee has appreciated over 2.5 per cent against the dollar. The return of FPIs can partly be explained by the decline in global crude-oil prices and concerns over the valuations of artificial intelligence (AI) companies, particularly after the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of the United States Congress. It is argued that the pace of AI development may now slow. Since India was not part of the big AI play, market rotation is benefitting it.  However, strong buying by FPIs in one month should not be seen as a trend reversal. Net FPI equity flows for the year are still about negative $15 billion. Foreign investors took out about $18.9 billion in 2025 as well. While crude oil prices have declined, a resumption of the war, which cannot be ruled out completely, could push prices up again. As demonstrated over the past several months, higher oil prices tend to significantly change macroeconomic management dynamics in India. However, even if oil prices settle at the pre-war level, it may not completely reverse the dynamics on the external front.  There is a view that a decline in oil prices will lead to substantial capital inflows, resulting in a significant strengthening of the rupee. This may be an overly optimistic assumption. It is worth remembering that India faced a balance of payments (BoP) deficit in the past two financial years as well, despite much lower oil prices. A substantial shift in capital flow, to a large extent, is usually driven by global interest rates, particularly in the US. Here are two examples. First, as interest rates were reduced following the outbreak of the pandemic and large central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, pumped in liquidity to support the financial system and economic activity, capital inflows into India surged. India’s foreign exchange (FX) reserves increased by over $100 billion in 2020-21. Second, when interest rates were raised by large central banks in a coordinated fashion in 2022 to tackle inflation, India’s FX reserves declined by over $100 billion between February and November 2022.  Things stabilised thereafter, and the RBI rebuilt its reserves. However, external conditions for India have been challenging for some time despite not running a large current account deficit (CAD). Given the persistent capital outflows, there was a risk of a BoP deficit for the third year in a row, which prompted the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to announce concessional swap schemes in June.  Data for the first half of the ongoing financial year shows that India has registered a BoP surplus of about $66.8 billion, largely on account of inflows under the swap schemes. The return of the FPIs is definitely a big relief, but the outcomes on the external front in the near to medium term will depend on several factors.  First, the direction of energy prices. An early agreement between Iran and the US will help bring down crude oil prices sustainably. This will not only help contain the CAD but also encourage foreign investors to look at India more positively. Things will obviously worsen if the attacks resume.  Second, the pace of global AI  buildout. A slowdown will help India as investors will look for alternative opportunities. However, if the correction in the valuations of AI-related companies becomes disorderly or the so-called AI bubble bursts, external financial conditions could worsen significantly for India. In case of a sudden increase in risk-aversion in the global financial system, capital tends to flow out of emerging markets. The 2008 global financial crisis is a good example.  Third, interest rates in the US. There are two main drivers here. One, although lower energy prices are a relief, inflation in the US has been running above target for over five years, and the Fed has reiterated its commitment to bringing it down. Financial markets expect the Fed to increase interest rates further in its December meeting. Moreover, a reduction can safely be ruled out until inflation gets sustainably close to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Two, as argued in this space earlier, the budget deficit and public debt have increased structurally in the US. Higher funding requirements of the US government in the foreseeable future will significantly influence the cost of money, keeping it elevated. In fact, high levels of public debt in most advanced economies will constrain the flow of capital to emerging markets.  Note that all these factors are exogenous and India cannot do much about them. However, it needs to be prepared to deal with their effects. What India can do is improve its competitiveness to attract and retain capital. In the first half of the current financial year, net foreign direct investment was at $8.8 billion. It was a marginal improvement over the previous year, but this number needs to go up substantially. Notwithstanding the gush of inflows this month, external financial conditions are likely to remain challenging in the foreseeable future. India will need to work on its internal drivers much more effectively to strengthen its external position. New proposed tariffs by the US add to the challenges.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: State finances look stronger, but hidden risks threaten their resilience
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / State finances look stronger, but hidden risks threaten their resilienceState finances look stronger, but hidden risks threaten their resilience

Temporary revenue surges risk masking deeper structural vulnerabilities

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Kavita Rao6 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 9:38 PM ISTHeadline fiscal metrics across India’s state governments currently project an image of post-pandemic resilience. Buoyed by accelerating tax collections and moderated revenue expenditure, state treasuries appear, on the surface, to have regained their balance. Yet, beneath these reassuring top-line figures lies an emerging structural crisis. Key concerns include tightening monetary conditions, growing reliance on off-budget liabilities, unbudgeted climate-related shocks, and impending revenue erosion arising from the transition to clean energy.  Early evidence of fiscal recovery  At first glance, the fiscal indicators for the current financial year present a compelling story of recovery1. Data for the early months of April to August reveals that total revenue receipts across major states grew by 13.1 per cent year-on-year, up dramatically from 6.2 per cent during the same period in the previous financial year.  This momentum was anchored by own tax revenue, which expanded at 14.8 per cent, compared to 5.5 per cent previously, while own non-tax revenue surged by 28.1 per cent. Furthermore, states demonstrated commendable expenditure discipline, moderating revenue expenditure growth to 4.7 per cent while elevating capital outlays by 10.4 per cent to build productive infrastructure.  However, this apparent strength conceals severe structural vulnerabilities. The macroeconomic environment is shifting. As inflation concerns persist — driven by agricultural disruptions and volatile global oil prices — the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) Monetary Policy Committee shifted its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening, initiating a 25-basis-point hike in the repo rate. Given the persistence of inflation, with retail inflation crossing 6 per cent — upper tolerance limit of the RBI — further increase in interest rates is anticipated. This is further reinforced by the expectation of an increase in interest rates by the US Federal Reserve as well.  Over the last 12 months, the yield on 10-year Government of India (GoI) bonds has increased from 6.54 per cent in November 2025 to a peak of 7.38 per cent in October 2026, before declining to 7.21 per cent in November 2026. Despite this moderation, yields remain distinctly higher than their levels a year ago. State development loans (SDLs) typically trade at a margin over the GoI bonds. The yield on SDLs of similar tenure crossed 8 per cent in October 2026 before declining marginally to 7.91 per cent in November 2026.  This firming of sovereign and subnational bond yields inflicts an immediate double blow on state finances. Fresh borrowings required to bridge fiscal deficits must now be contracted at yields hovering around 8 per cent. Simultaneously, states face the additional burden of costly debt rollovers. As maturing debt issued during lower-rate cycles comes up for refinancing, reissued paper is incurring yield that is 20 to 40 basis points higher.  Structural fractures: Discoms, energy, and climate  The fragility of state finances is further compounded by deep structural liabilities in the energy and environmental sectors.  The ₹7.4 trillion power sector drag: The power distribution sector remains the largest single threat to state fiscal stability. The Power Finance Corporations’ Performance Report on power utilities indicates a systematic increase in outstanding liabilities of discoms, from  ₹6.14 trillion in 2021-22 to ₹7.58 trillion in 2023-24. There is a marginal decline during 2024-25 to ₹7.26 trillion. Of this stock of outstanding liabilities, ₹7.11 trillion is attributable to state discoms.  Clearly, there has been some improvement in the performance of the power sector, as reflected in timely realisation of subsidies, a reduction in aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses, and an improvement in billing efficiency, to name a few indicators. Yet the scale of these losses continues to represent a stress point for state finances. As may be noted, these losses are severely concentrated in some key states:  High-stress states (liabilities ≥ 2 per cent of gross state domestic product): Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh.  Moderate-stress states (liabilities between 1.5 per cent and 2 per cent of gross state domestic product): Maharashtra and Karnataka.  Additional borrowing to meet current and capital needs for this sector will remain a source of concern for the state governments. The immediate liabilities do not rest with the state, but the contingent liability does rest here, through explicit and implicit guarantees.  The decarbonisation tax trap  Looking ahead, the global and domestic push towards transport electrification introduces a structural revenue crisis. State governments currently rely on petroleum sales taxes for about 20 per cent of their total tax revenue. The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) threatens to dismantle this fiscal foundation.  Without a clear strategy to decouple state budgets from fossil fuel taxation and calibrate the rollout of EV incentives, decarbonisation will precipitate a permanent structural revenue deficit.  Unbudgeted climate shocks  Compounding these energy dynamics is the rising frequency of extreme weather events. Recent El Niño phenomena have triggered widespread droughts, forcing state administrations to roll out unbudgeted relief measures. Ground-level climate mapping underscores the scale of exposure:  The Council on Energy, Environment and Water study identifies Maharashtra and Karnataka as acutely drought-prone.  The India Meteorological Department Hazard Atlas flags Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Karnataka as highly vulnerable to severe drought.  When natural disasters strike, states not only suffer immediate contractions in own tax revenue due to impaired agricultural productivity, but they must also mobilise significant counterpart funding. For key central assistance schemes, such as the VB-G RAM G rural infrastructure initiative, states are required to furnish 40 per cent of total expenditure from their own funds, pulling administrative and financial resources away from long-term development towards emergency relief. Investing in climate-proofing agriculture should, therefore, be a priority. This would involve not only new technologies, but also dissemination efforts to support their adoption on a large scale.  India’s states cannot afford to mistake temporary revenue surges for structural solvency. Focused interventions to address emerging liabilities will, therefore, be critical going forward.

entry.title: A commitment to strengthen our Constitution, writes PM Narendra Modi
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A commitment to strengthen our Constitution, writes PM Narendra ModiA commitment to strengthen our Constitution, writes PM Narendra Modi

"For crores of Indians, including me, the Constitution of India is an inseparable part of our life journeys"

Prime Minister Narendra Modi calls for strengthening constitutional values and placing India First in national endeavours.

Narendra Modi New Delhi 7 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 6:05 AM ISTOn 26th November 1949, the Constituent Assembly adopted our Constitution. Today, we remember Dr Rajendra Prasad, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar and every member of the Constituent Assembly. Their greatness lay in drawing extensively from the rich traditions and civilisational wisdom of Bharat while framing a modern Constitution. For a nation as diverse as Bharat, with its numerous faiths, languages, customs and schools of thought, it is important that the Constitution have a resonance far beyond the precincts of Parliament and the courts. Our endeavour has been to deepen its connect with the collective consciousness of our people, especially our youth and strengthen the spirit of unity essential to India’s bright future. That is why over a decade ago, our government decided to mark 26th November as Constitution Day.  For crores of Indians, including me, the Constitution of India is an inseparable part of our life journeys. Whenever I look back at my childhood, the humble circumstances in which I grew up, the struggles that were a part of everyday life, I am filled with an overwhelming sense of gratitude towards our Constitution. That a child born into a family of modest means, with no privileges or advantages of birth, could one day be entrusted with the responsibility of serving the world’s largest democracy speaks volumes about how extraordinary our Constitution is. It is due to our Constitution that circumstances of one’s birth no longer determine the limits of one’s future.  In our own humble way, we have sought to repay this debt of gratitude by streng-thening our Constitution. The distinguished constitutional scholar Granville Austin described our Constitution as “first and foremost a social document.” The quest for social and economic justice runs through the very fabric of our Constitution. Thus, what can be more satisfying than working towards the realisation of this cherished vision of the makers of our Constitution? 

Also Read

Bollywood union asks PM Modi to bar Netflix's Pakistani series in India

Cong to hold 'vote chori' protest marches across India on Constitution Day

Nepal PM's India visit signals a thaw, but key demands remain unmetpremium

PM Modi, German Chancellor Merz discuss regional, global developments

India, Nepal announce 21 outcomes, ₹15,000 cr economic aid package

A recent World Bank report highlights that nearly 500 million Indians have moved out of poverty. Breaking free from generations of deprivation, crores of parents can now dream of a better future for their children. When PM Awas Yojana ensures a family moves from a thatched roof to a pucca home, the constitutional promise of dignity acquires meaning.  When Ujjwala Yojana frees a mother from the hardships of a smoke-filled kitchen, we advance the ideals of equality and well-being. When Ayushman Bharat enables a poor family to access quality health care without the fear of debt, social justice becomes a lived reality. When MUDRA and PM-SVANidhi provide collateral-free credit to small entrepreneurs and street vendors, economic justice finds expression. When digital technology and platforms like UPI transcend all divides and place opportunities once available to a privileged few within the reach of every citizen, we advance the constitutional ideal of inclusivity. There are many more manifestations of this constitutional vision. The list of amendments we brought can be viewed through the same prism. The 101st Amendment ushered in GST, a long-awaited reform. The 102nd Amendment granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes, fulfilling a long-standing dream of the marginalised sections of society. The 103rd Amendment received broad social acceptance. By providing reservation to Economically Weaker Sections, it addressed the long-overlooked aspirations of economically disadvantaged families from communities outside the existing reservation framework. For the first time since 1950, an updated version of our Constitution is now available in all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule. This has brought our Constitution closer to the people. Even after our Constitution came into force in 1950, we continued to be governed by the colonial penal code dating back to the 1860s. With the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, we have sought to bring about a fundamental shift in our criminal justice system, moving from the colonial emphasis on punishment (Dand) to a citizen-centric pursuit of justice (Nyay). Over the past decade, we have laid special emphasis on Kartavya, or the duties of a citizen. Our civilisation has always emphasised the responsibilities that accompany every role in society. The spirit of Kartavya has found expression in several mass movements, from Swachh Bharat to water conservation and environmental protection. However, there is another reality that I feel compelled to share. There have been occasions in our history when those entrusted with upholding the Constitution chose to weaken it. Ironically, they are the same people who had the opportunity to govern India for five decades. This year marks 75 years since the First Amendment of 1951, when a government that was not popularly elected used its majority in the Provisional Parliament to restrict fundamental freedoms. Its timing, barely months before India’s first general election, proves that it was intended to influence the electoral process and stifle public opposition. It is also 50 years since the 42nd Amendment at the height of the Emergency. This curtailed judicial review and fundamentally altered the balance of institutional powers. I would also urge youngsters to study the 38th and 39th Amendments to know what a power-hungry and anti-constitutional leadership can do. The repeated misuse of Article 356 to dismiss elected state governments presents another troubling chapter. One party has the dubious record of imposing Article 356 almost a hundred times and one former Prime Minister has scored a half-century in this field. The makers of our Constitution had hoped that it would be implemented in letter and spirit across India. But, for over 70 years, Articles 370 and 35A did not allow the full Constitution to be implemented in Jammu and Kashmir, thus trampling over the rights of SC, ST, OBC communities and women. It was only in 2019 that this historical wrong was corrected. For decades, in several parts of India, particularly in tribal areas, Naxalites used the might of the gun to deny the poorest people the rights guaranteed to them by our Constitution. The successful elimination of Naxalism this year is particularly heartwarming because it has ensured that the poorest of the poor can finally exercise their constitutional rights without fear. Now, we are left only with ‘Dimagi Naxals’, far removed from the realities of our times but persistent in their efforts to derail our growth trajectory. It is most appalling that the biggest party in the Opposition wants to reduce OBC reservation and bring Muslim reservations, something the makers of our Constitution, notably Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar, were totally against. The journey of our Constitution would be incomplete without recognising the remarkable women who helped shape it. But what happened earlier this year should fill our hearts with shame. A legislation aimed at giving women adequate representation in legislative bodies was disallowed from being passed by the one Opposition party, once again showing its disdain for constitutional values. I assure the Nari Shakti of India that no force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them. Our constitutional democracy has a clearly defined role for the Opposition. Sadly, the leading Opposition party seems to have become more of an Avrodh Paksh (obstructionist) than a Virodh Paksh (Opposition). They should know that disrupting democratic processes is no substitute for discharging constitutional responsibilities. Today, India stands at a defining moment. As we work towards Viksit Bharat by 2047, two simple yet powerful principles can guide our collective endeavours: India First in our thinking and Kartavya (duties) in our actions. With these as our guiding principles and the Constitution as our source of strength, we can secure a bright future for generations to come. The writer is the Prime Minister of IndiaDisclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: The Nvidia moment: Business, public affairs and the unfolding AI shift
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The Nvidia moment: Business, public affairs and the unfolding AI shiftThe Nvidia moment: Business, public affairs and the unfolding AI shift

AI is transforming businesses and society, but India must focus on ethical governance, institutional leadership and public trust alongside technological adoption

premium

Artificial intelligence technology and digital innovation shaping the future of businesses and industries (Photo: Shuttershock)

Ajay Khanna10 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 11:13 PM IST“Buy Nvidia, sell Nvidia, hold Nvidia”. Over the last few weeks, it has been difficult to escape these conversations. Turn on the television — American, European, Indian, Asian, any channel — and there is another discussion about Nvidia. Open any social media platform and there is a fresh wave of commentary, analysis, and predictions. At business meetings or family conversations over coffee, artificial intelligence (AI) seems to find its way into almost every conversation.  I have been travelling across the United States — from Chicago to San Diego and Los Angeles — and have been struck by the scale of this attention. Nvidia has become a particularly visible reference point, but the conversation is much bigger. It is about AI, the companies developing it, the growing ecosystem around it and, above all, the transformation it could bring. In four decades of working in public affairs, I cannot recall seeing this level of public attention around technological development and the companies associated with it. Let me clarify that I am not a stock market investor or trader. This is not an investment view or a recommendation to buy or sell any company. My interests are quite different. I wanted to understand what was driving this extraordinary attention and, more importantly, what it told us about the changes taking place around us.  I had experienced a similar moment of curiosity earlier this year, in January 2026, at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting in Davos. AI was already a major subject of discussion across the meeting. But walking along a promenade, I was struck by the sheer visibility of AI companies, their branding, and advertisements. They seemed to be everywhere. Even the consulting firms’ outreach focused on how they could help corporations build AI applications. I wrote about this from Davos, reflecting on what this growing presence might mean for business and technology. A few months later, travelling across America, I find that the conversation has become even more pervasive.  What has struck me most is the speed of AI’s evolution and adoption. We often think of technological change as something that will shape the future. With AI, that future seems to be arriving much faster than many of us anticipated. Its applications are becoming increasingly visible across businesses, professions, education, healthcare, public services, skills, and everyday life. Sitting in Chicago, I began asking some basic questions. What exactly is AI? How does it work? Why has it become so central to the global business conversation? I began reading, asking questions, and trying to understand.  I also started experimenting through conversations with ChatGPT. I would ask a question, follow it with another, sometimes challenge an answer, and occasionally move into an entirely different subject. It was an interesting experience — not simply receiving information, but using a new tool to connect ideas and explore subjects in different ways. I was learning about AI while, in a small way, learning through AI itself. The more I learnt, the more intrigued I became — not just by the technology, but by the scale of change it could bring to business, society and the way we live and work.  AI in public affairs  Perhaps my professional journey had something to do with where my curiosity took me next. As the founder of the Public Affairs Forum of India, I have spent much of my working life at the intersection of business, government and society. Over the years, I have seen how public policy shapes business opportunities, how business decisions influence society and how constructive engagement between stakeholders helps build trust.  AI brings a new dimension to these relationships. Its impact will not be confined to the companies developing the technology. It will influence how businesses operate, how governments deliver services, how professions evolve, and how society responds to change. The implications will extend well beyond technology — to public policy, regulation, employment, skills, competitiveness and public trust.  From a public affairs perspective, this is particularly interesting. The adoption of AI will inevitably bring businesses into closer engagement with government, regulators, employees, customers and communities. Understanding these different perspectives, and how they interact, will be an important part of navigating the transformation.  One thought that kept returning to me was the distinction between building a successful business and building an enduring institution. India has an impressive history of entrepreneurial achievement. Many of our most successful businesses have been built through the vision, conviction, and extraordinary energy of their founders. We have also seen family businesses evolve across generations, professionalise their management, and become institutions much larger than the individuals who started them.  This is a fascinating journey, but the transition from founder-led success to institution-building is not always easy. It involves balancing legacy with change, ownership with professional management, and individual vision with collective responsibility. This is particularly so for the startups.  The qualities that help build a business are not necessarily the same as those needed to sustain an institution across generations. An enduring institution needs more than a successful business model. It needs a culture, a purpose, and values that continue to guide it even as its leadership changes.  This becomes particularly relevant as Indian family businesses navigate generational transitions and entrepreneurial ventures grow into larger, more complex organisations. AI adds another dimension to this challenge. The ability to adapt to technological change will increasingly depend not just on investment in technology, but also on an organisation’s people, culture, leadership and capacity to evolve. It is not about choosing between family ownership and professional management. It is about finding the right balance between entrepreneurial spirit, professional capability and institutional continuity.  A thought worth reflecting on is this: A company should ultimately be bigger than its chief executive officer, stronger than its founder, and capable of carrying its values across generations. Leadership creates success. I firmly believe institution-building gives that success a longer life.  Governance and ethics  Governance and ethics are often discussed in formal terms — boards, committees, policies, compliance and reporting. All have their place. But I have increasingly come to believe that the real story lies in the culture of an organisation. What happens when someone raises an uncomfortable question? Can an employee express a concern without worrying about the consequences? Are difficult decisions examined independently? Do values hold firm when commercial pressures are high?  These are not questions that can be answered simply by reading a company’s governance report. They become visible in everyday decisions and in how people behave when nobody is watching. As organisations begin to use AI in more aspects of their operations and decision-making, these questions acquire a new significance. How much should we rely on technology? Where does human judgement remain essential? Who is accountable when an automated decision has unintended consequences?  These are questions worth exploring in boardrooms and leadership discussions as organisations consider the opportunities AI offers. Technology may evolve rapidly, but the importance of judgement, responsibility and accountability will remain. Companies do not operate in isolation. Their decisions affect employees, customers, investors, governments, regulators, communities, and civil society. In my experience, understanding this wider ecosystem — and engaging constructively with it — is central to building lasting relationships and public trust.  As AI becomes more pervasive, these relationships are likely to become even more important. Its adoption may raise questions about jobs and skills, data and privacy, consumer interests, transparency and the way decisions are made. Stakeholders will naturally have different perspectives and expectations.  For businesses, understanding these perspectives will be part of navigating the transition. It is not simply a matter of adopting a technology and communicating the decision afterwards. There is value in listening, exchanging views and understanding the wider implications as the adoption process unfolds.  This is where public affairs has an important contribution to make: connecting business priorities with the larger public policy and societal environment. Constructive engagement with government, regulators, industry bodies, academia, and civil society can help organisations understand emerging issues and contribute to the conversations shaping the future.  Ultimately, trust is built over time through the way organisations conduct themselves and engage with the world around them. As AI changes how businesses function, the importance of these relationships is unlikely to diminish.  India’s AI moment  For India, the possibilities are enormous. AI could improve public service delivery, enhance productivity, strengthen healthcare and education, and contribute to the competitiveness of Indian businesses.  There are already important discussions underway in government, regulatory institutions, and think tanks. How should India approach AI regulation? What safeguards are needed around privacy, transparency, bias and accountability? How do we encourage innovation while protecting the wider public interest?  These are important questions, and the conversations will continue to evolve as the technology develops.  But there is another question that interests me: while these discussions are taking place in policy circles, are Indian businesses and organisations giving equal attention to these issues? As companies accelerate AI adoption, are they also considering its implications for employees, customers and other stakeholders? Are ethical governance, accountability, and responsible use finding their way into boardroom discussions? Are organisations thinking about how their people, culture and institutional processes will adapt to the pace of change?  I do not suggest that these questions have simple answers, or that every organisation will approach them in the same way. Sectors will have different experiences and priorities. But it will be interesting to see how the conversations between business, government, and society develop.  For India, the opportunity is not just to adopt AI, but also to participate in shaping the environment in which it grows and is used. That will require perspectives from technology, business, public policy, academia and civil society.  Conversations ahead  This is, in many ways, only the beginning of my own exploration. I look forward to exploring the fascinating intersection of AI and public affairs more deeply in the months ahead.  I am particularly curious about how these conversations will unfold in India: how policymakers and regulators will approach this rapidly evolving technology, how Indian companies and institutions will embrace it while thinking through ethical governance and accountability, and how business and society will navigate the opportunities and challenges together.  As I return to Davos in January 2027, I will be watching with even greater curiosity. AI was already a prominent subject at the Annual Meeting in January 2026. What will the conversations look like this time? Will they move further beyond the technology and investment story to the larger questions of business transformation, public policy, governance and society? And how much of what is being discussed will help shape the global agenda?  I suspect the most interesting conversations are still ahead of us. I look forward to listening, learning, and sharing more reflections. For now, I am left with a simple thought: the pace of technological change may be extraordinary, but the human questions around leadership, judgement, responsibility and trust remain as relevant as ever.  And perhaps that is where the most interesting conversation about AI really begins — not just with what the technology can do, but with how businesses, institutions and societies choose to understand it, adopt it and shape the future together.

entry.title: 2026's CEO transitions test continuity, governance, and strategic change
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / 2026's CEO transitions test continuity, governance, and strategic change2026's CEO transitions test continuity, governance, and strategic change

From abrupt exits and dramatic comebacks to planned successions, the global corporate world saw many leadership changes, with all eyes now on the new chiefs as they navigate an evolving business lands

premium

Corporate leaders at a boardroom meeting, representing leadership transitions in global businesses (Representative Image)

Shailesh Dobhal5 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 10:52 PM ISTHow will 2026 be remembered by the business world globally? For its record-breaking initial public offerings (IPO), from Anthropic’s $83 billion IPO, the world’s largest, to SpaceX’s $75 billion offering. Closer home, amid a record rush, India too witnessed its biggest-ever offering in Jio Platform’s over ₹30,000 crore IPO, and the debut of the long-awaited National Stock Exchange’s IPO, valued at ₹22,000 crore.  The corporate governance saga playing out between Tata Sons and Tata Trusts over control of the eponymous $200 billion salt-to-software conglomerate also consumed much of the business press’s attention through the year, with no endgame in sight. The continued march of the artificial intelligence (AI) juggernaut — from the humongous money raised from public and private markets and its concomitant impact on the global cost and availability of capital to unauthorised hacks by agents of leading global AI firms raising fears of not just technological disruptions but an existential threat to humanity — kept everyone, from markets to regulators, on the edge of their seats.  Leadership transitions across some global and Indian firms were no less important, though one grabbed the headlines for all the wrong reasons — a quick exit and an equally dramatic return within a fortnight. Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive officer of AI chipmaker Nvidia, the world’s largest firm by market capitalisation, set the markets on a rollercoaster amid a spy-romance scandal.  If one were to bucket the big leadership transitions across global and Indian firms this year, the most consequential ones would fall into one of two categories:  Continuity Inc: These are cases where the firms transitioned existing leaders or founders into bigger oversight roles even as new blood, albeit a company insider, was inducted into the corner room. Think Airtel, the country’s second-largest telco by subscribers, where a planned succession saw former chief operating officer Shashwat Sharma take over as chief executive officer (CEO) in January, even as long-term CEO Gopal Vittal transitioned to a vice-chairman role.  Founder of food delivery firm Eternal, Deepinder Goyal, vacated his group CEO position in favour of its quick-delivery division’s co-founder Albinder Dhindsa to take on the role of vice-chairman in February.  Globally too, there were many such planned moves. John Ternus took over from Tim Cook, CEO for 15 years, in September at Apple, with Mr Cook taking on the executive chairman’s mantle. Spotify founder and CEO for two decades, Daniel Ek, moved to the executive chairman’s position, with his long-time deputies Alex Norstrom and Gustav Soderstrom moving in as co-CEOs in January. At Coca-Cola, incumbent CEO James Quincey moved to the executive chairman role, handing the reins to COO Henrique Braun in March.  Shantanu Narayen, Adobe’s CEO for around two decades, will move to the role of executive chair as Anil Chakravarthy takes over as CEO, effective December 1. Josh D’Amaro replaced Bob Iger as The Walt Disney Company’s CEO nine months ahead of schedule in March, with Mr Iger remaining associated with the entertainment and theme park company as a board member. And legendary investor, 96-year-old Warren Buffett, often referred to as the Oracle of Omaha, finally bowed out in September from Berkshire Hathaway, the trillion-dollar financial conglomerate he had led since 1965, letting his son Howard Buffett take over as chairman, with the senior Buffett taking on the role of chairman emeritus.  To be sure, such orderly transition of an incumbent into a mentor and/or oversight role is not always an unalloyed gift. Handled properly, it can ensure stability of the corporate structure and strategy, and add shareholder value. On the flip side, if the roles are not strictly adhered to, in letter and spirit, the presence of the iconic or long-serving CEO can very easily undermine and constrict the newcomer to the detriment of the organisation and its stakeholders.      Closely-watched transitions: These are cases of big, visible firms where there is ostensibly a need for a strategic/structural pivot, and the incumbent invariably moves out making way for a company outsider or a long-time deputy. The country’s largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank, saw rival ICICI Bank veteran Anup Bagchi take charge as its MD & CEO in October, succeeding Sashidhar Jagdishan.  Recall that the bank’s chairman, Atanu Chakraborty, resigned in March, raising concerns (unsubstantiated) over certain business practices that he said were not aligned with his “personal values and ethics”. At the loss-making, crisis-hit Air India, incumbent CEO Campbell Wilson was replaced by former Ethiopian Airlines veteran Tewolde Gebremariam in August-September.  The world’s largest physical retailer Walmart saw its CEO of over a decade, Doug McMillon, retire in January, handing over charge to its US chief, John Furner, just as agentic commerce is taking shape.  And energy major BP appointed Meg O’Neill, its first external hire for the CEO position and the first woman to lead one of the world’s top five oil majors, replacing its CEO of just over two years, Murray Auchincloss, in April. Though proven leaders in their previous jobs, all eyes will be on these new chiefs as they navigate the corporate labyrinth.
